name: message-router
intent: Route each message to the destination that its contents or metadata select, keeping the routing decision in one replaceable place so producers and consumers stay unaware of the topology.
problem: Where a message goes depends on the message: a fixed wiring between producer and consumer no longer works, and letting every producer pick a destination or every consumer filter the stream it receives scatters the routing decision across the system, so a new message type or a changed destination forces edits in many components.
context: Message-based integration where a Pipes and Filters chain connects several destinations over message channels, where the destination of a message follows from its type, headers or key fields, where routing rules evolve independently of the business logic of the endpoints, and where the message itself must arrive unmodified. Applies at integration boundaries, inside a broker topology, or in-process between channel-like queues; the routing criteria must be expressible as a decision over message metadata, not as a transformation of the payload.
benefits: The destination criteria live in a single location: when message types are added, destinations are added, or rules change, only the router logic changes and every other component stays untouched.
Producers are decoupled from consumers - a producer writes to one input channel and never learns who receives the message, so destinations can be reorganized without redeploying producers.
The router does not modify the message (a key property of the pattern): routing stays separate from transformation, and the same router serves any number of flows.
Surrounding filters remain unaware that a router is present: because it behaves like a filter in a Pipes and Filters architecture, the decision can be inserted into an existing channel chain.
Routing becomes a testable and auditable unit: the rule set can be exercised as a decision matrix, and per-destination counters make the topology observable from one place.
It is the stable base of the whole routing family (Content-Based Router, Message Filter, Recipient List, Dynamic Router), so a system grows route by route without re-architecting the flow.
tradeoffs: Single point of contention: every message traverses the router, so its availability and throughput bound the whole flow, and an outage of the router stops the pipeline (replication and failover become part of the design).

The topology becomes implicit: reading a producer no longer reveals the destinations, so impact analysis, capacity planning and on-call debugging require routing observability (counts and latencies per route).

Routing rules accrete domain knowledge and drift into a god component or an ad-hoc rules engine; once rules must change at runtime, the plain router should be replaced by a Dynamic Router or an explicit rules engine.
The router couples to the message contract because the decision reads headers or key fields, so changes to that metadata ripple into routing everywhere, including into tests.
Silent misrouting is the default failure mode: a message that matches no rule is dropped unless a default branch exists, and a subtly wrong rule is invisible without per-destination metrics.

An extra hop and a rule evaluation per message add latency and a second hand-off that can fail independently (publish succeeded, routing failed), which broker-side routing avoids by pushing the decision into the exchange.
A routing matrix must be maintained in addition to the endpoint tests, and the interaction of overlapping rules (precedence, first-match-wins) is a recurring source of defects.

participants.responsibility: Consumes messages from the input channel, evaluates the routing rules against message metadata, and republishes each message unchanged to the selected output channel(s); it never transforms the payload.

The ordered predicate/destination pairs (or the routing function) that implement the decision; they are the one place where destination criteria are maintained and are ideally data (table, config) rather than code.
The single inbound channel the router consumes from; producers write here and know nothing about the destinations.
The destination channels the router publishes to; each message is republished to exactly one, or to several when the rule set fans out.
The routed data plus the metadata (type, headers, key fields) the decision is based on; it reaches the destination byte-for-byte unchanged.
The consumers on the output channels; they process a message stream that has already been selected for them and remain unaware of the router.

use_cases: Order intake: route orders by type, region or channel to payment, fulfilment, fraud-check and manual-review queues without teaching the order service about any of them.
Log and event routing: publish on a severity/facility key and let broker bindings deliver to storage, alerting and audit consumers (the classic syslog-shaped topic topology).
Multi-tenant messaging: route by tenant id to per-tenant queues or partitions so quotas, isolation and retention can differ per tenant.
Integration between legacy and modern systems: route messages for migrated entities to the new service and the rest to the legacy interface (or the reverse during a migration window).
API gateway / broker mediation: map protocol messages to the service that owns the contract, keeping the client unaware of the service topology.
Stream partitioning for processing affinity: route by entity key so all events of one entity reach the same worker and stay ordered.

RabbitMQ exchange routing: publish an unchanged message with a stable routing key to a direct or topic exchange, whose bindings deliver it to matching queues without coupling the producer to queue names or topology.

Apache Camel Choice EIP: evaluate ordered predicates and send the exchange to the first matching branch, using an explicit otherwise route for unmatched messages while leaving transformation to later processors.

Spring Integration channel routing: use HeaderValueRouter or PayloadTypeRouter to map a message to a channel, with a default-output-channel or explicit unresolved-route policy instead of silently losing the message.
avoid_when: There is exactly one producer and one consumer and the destination never varies - a direct channel or a plain function call is simpler and has no hop.
The routing decision is already available at the call site (the caller knows the destination) and no second consumer will ever care - hard-wiring the destination is honest and cheaper.

The set of recipients is data rather than a decision - use Recipient List; the rules must change at runtime - use Dynamic Router; the need is to drop or trim messages rather than choose between destinations - use Message Filter or Content Filter.
A consumer can select what it wants itself (Selective Consumer) or the broker already routes by subscription, so a central application-level router would only duplicate the decision.
The flow is a single high-volume pipeline whose only variation is a transformation step - the router adds latency without buying decoupling.
anti_patterns: The transformer router: the component that routes and also rewrites, enriches or reformats the message, breaking the pattern's invariant that routing leaves the message untouched (use Message Translator for that step).
The god router: rules accumulate business policy until the router knows every domain rule; policy belongs in a rules engine or a Dynamic Router, or in the services themselves.
Producer-side routing: each sender picks the destination and publishes directly to it, which re-couples producers to consumers and spreads the criteria the router exists to centralize.
Routing by parsing the message body, so every payload schema change becomes a routing outage and untrusted input reaches the decision logic.
No-route black hole: rules without a default branch, silently discarding anything that does not match.
Load balancing disguised as routing: round-robin between destinations is Competing Consumers or a dispatcher, not a routing decision.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: choosing a destination is one responsibility, transformation and business processing are others.
Single source of truth: destination criteria live in exactly one place, the rule set.
Information hiding / loose coupling: producers know only the input channel, consumers only their own output channel.
Open/closed principle: new message types and destinations are added by extending the rules, not by editing participants.
Policy separated from mechanism: the rules (policy) are data, the routing loop (mechanism) stays generic and stateless.
best_practices: Keep routing rules declarative and externalized (table or configuration) so a route change is reviewed and deployed like data, not buried in code.
Always define the unmatched case: a default destination, otherwise a Dead Letter Channel, with an alert on its depth.
Route on stable, typed metadata (message type, headers, correlation and partition keys) rather than free text in the body.
Leave the message unmodified - no enrichment, no normalization - and place a Message Translator after the route when the destination needs a different shape.
Make the router stateless and idempotent so instances can be replicated, and monitor per-route counts, latency and error rates.
Keep rules mutually exclusive or explicitly ordered, and document the precedence: first-match-wins semantics differ from a rules engine's.
Size the rule set for review: when it stops fitting one page or changes weekly, move it to a Dynamic Router or a rule engine.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Message Router, in the Message Routing chapter.
